h1: Beer with fried fish and chips the British way
title: Beer With Fish and Chips the British Way | Craft Beer School
desc: Why bitter and pale ale suit fried fish and chips, what carbonation and vinegar do to the pairing and how to try it in India.
teaser: Batter, salt and malt vinegar need a beer that scrubs the palate and keeps you coming back.
standfirst: Fish and chips with a pint of bitter is one of the oldest pairings in the pub. It works for clear reasons: fat, salt, acid and carbonation. Here is the logic, plus how to get the same effect with Indian fried fish.
sections: Why fried food and beer get along

Deep frying coats everything in fat. Fat dulls the palate: after three or four bites of battered cod, the fish tastes less of fish and more of oil. Beer resets that in two ways.

Carbonation lifts fat off the tongue. Hop bitterness cuts through what is left. That is the 'cut' in pairing language. A beer carbonated at around 2.0 to 2.5 volumes of CO2, which covers most bottled ales and lagers, does the job well. Cask bitter in a British pub is softer, nearer 1.0 to 1.5 volumes. It leans more on bitterness and malt to clean up. Our guide on how carbonation changes the way a beer tastes explains why that difference is so noticeable.
The classic pint: bitter or pale ale

In Britain the default is a best bitter or a pale ale, around 3.8 to 5% ABV with 25 to 40 IBU. That range is the sweet spot. The malt has enough biscuit and caramel to echo the golden batter. The hops are earthy and herbal rather than tropical, so they sit behind the food.

An English pale ale brewed with Maris Otter malt and Fuggle or East Kent Golding hops is close to the ideal. If your local taproom does an ESB, that works too, though at 5.5% and up it starts to compete with the fish.

The British pint glass matters less than people think, but it does hold a good head. If you want to know why the nonic has that bulge, see our piece on the nonic and the tulip pint.
Malt vinegar and salt change everything

The chip shop shakes salt and malt vinegar over everything. Both affect the beer.

Salt suppresses bitterness and makes malt taste sweeter. That is why a fairly bitter ale tastes balanced next to salty chips but harsh on its own. Vinegar adds acid, which does the opposite: it sharpens bitterness. A heavy dose of vinegar with a 50 IBU IPA is too much bitterness meeting too much acid.

So the order of the day is moderate. A moderately bitter beer, moderately salted chips and a sensible splash of vinegar. If you love drowning your chips, choose a beer at the low end of the bitterness range or a clean lager.
Lager is a fair choice too

Plenty of people in Britain drink lager with their fish supper and they are not wrong. A crisp Pilsner at 4.5 to 5% with 25 to 35 IBU and high carbonation cuts fat brilliantly. What it lacks is the bready malt that echoes the batter.

A Vienna lager or a Märzen splits the difference: lager cleanliness with a little toasted malt. If you are pairing for a group with mixed tastes, a Vienna lager is the safe bet.
Taking the idea to Indian fried fish

India has its own fried fish traditions. The same logic applies. Amritsari fish in a besan batter with ajwain, Kerala-style fish fry with a red chilli and pepper rub and Goan rava fried fish are all fat plus salt plus a little acid from lime.

With besan batter and ajwain, a pale ale works much as it does with cod. With a hot red masala, the chilli changes the picture: alcohol and hop bitterness both make chilli feel hotter. Drop to a 4 to 4.5% lager or a wheat beer so the heat stays pleasant. Squeeze the lime on the fish rather than into the beer.
Mushy peas, tartare and the rest of the plate

A proper chip shop supper rarely stops at fish and chips. Mushy peas, tartare sauce, a pickled onion or a wedge of lemon all turn up. Each nudges the beer.

Tartare sauce is mayonnaise with capers and gherkins: more fat plus a sharp, briny edge. It pushes you towards a beer with a little more bitterness and carbonation, so a pale ale beats a soft cask mild here. Mushy peas are sweet and earthy and barely affect the pairing. A pickled onion is pure acid, so take a sip of water after it rather than judging the beer straight away.

Lemon is the gentler cousin of vinegar. A squeeze over the fish adds brightness that a hoppy pale ale with citrus notes picks up nicely. If you are choosing between vinegar and lemon and you have an IPA in hand, choose lemon. The citrus hop aroma meets the fruit without the harsh clash that malt vinegar brings.
Carbonation and bitterness are what you are tasting

The reason this pairing works is that the beer is doing a job, not just tasting nice. A trained taster can feel the carbonation lifting the fat and can tell when bitterness is fighting vinegar. Most drinkers just notice that one plate tastes better than the other.

Here is a first step. Next time you have fried fish, order two beers: one bitter or pale ale and one lager. Alternate them bite by bite. Note which one makes the fourth bite taste as good as the first. That beer is cutting the fat best for your palate.
faqs: What beer is traditional with fish and chips?
A British bitter or pale ale, usually 3.8 to 5% ABV. The malt echoes the batter and the bitterness cuts the fat.
Is lager good with fish and chips?
Yes. A crisp Pilsner cuts fat very well thanks to its high carbonation. It just has less malt to match the batter than a bitter does.
Yes. Vinegar adds acid, which makes bitter beers taste sharper. Heavy vinegar suits a less bitter beer.
What beer goes with Amritsari fish?
A pale ale or a clean lager. If the fish is very spicy, choose a lower alcohol, less bitter beer so the heat does not build.
